title: Collaborative Document Editor
prompt: Design a document editor where several people can type into the same document at the same time and see each other's changes and cursors live. It should keep full version history and let people keep editing while offline.

clarify.q: Plain text, rich text, or structured content like tables and embedded objects?
clarify.why: Rich text and tables multiply the operation types you must transform or merge. Plain text lets you explain the core with insert and delete only.

clarify.q: How many people edit one document at once, typically and at worst?
clarify.why: Two to five editors is the normal case. A shared all-hands doc with 200 editors decides whether one process per document is enough and how hard fan-out gets.

clarify.q: How long can someone stay offline and still merge cleanly?
clarify.why: Minutes of offline work is easy with a server-ordered algorithm. Days of offline work on both sides pushes you toward CRDTs, where merge does not depend on a shared base.
If the server cannot read operations it cannot transform them. That rules out server-side OT and forces a CRDT merged on clients.

clarify.q: What does version history mean: every keystroke, or named and periodic snapshots?
clarify.why: Keeping every op forever costs terabytes per day. Periodic revisions plus a bounded op log is far cheaper and is what most users actually browse.

clarify.q: Do comments, suggestions and permissions changes need to be live too?
clarify.why: Comments can ride a normal REST plus pub/sub path. Only document body edits need the ordered op pipeline.

clarify.q: What latency do people expect to see a teammate's keystroke?
clarify.why: Local typing must be instant (optimistic). Remote edits under about 200 ms feel live. That number sizes the batching interval and rules out polling.

functional: Several users edit one document concurrently. All replicas converge to the same content.
Local edits apply instantly, before any server round trip.
Users see collaborators' cursors, selections and who is present.
Users can browse and restore earlier versions of the document.
A user who goes offline keeps editing. Edits merge when they reconnect.
nonFunctional: Remote edits visible to other editors in p99 under 300 ms within a region.
No acknowledged edit is ever lost: an op is acked only after a durable write.
Convergence is guaranteed: same set of ops gives the same document on every replica.
Open a 1 MB document in under 1 s (load snapshot plus a short op tail).
99.95% availability for editing. Presence may degrade first.
outOfScope: Spreadsheet formulas and the calculation engine.
Sharing UI and the permissions model beyond a simple check on connect.

assumptions: 20 M daily active users, 2 M editing sessions open at peak
Average room size seen by a session: 3 editors (most docs have 1, a few have dozens)
Clients batch keystrokes and send at most one op message every 100 ms, about 1 message/s per session on average
One op message ≈ 100 bytes with metadata. Cursor updates throttled to at most 5/s, about 1/s on average
Average day runs at about one quarter of peak load

steps.label: Outbound fan-out at peak
steps.result: ≈ 4 M op deliveries/s, plus ≈ 4 M cursor deliveries/s

steps.label: WebSocket gateways
steps.math: 2 M connections / 50 k connections per box = 40 boxes
steps.result: ≈ 60 gateways with headroom for a zone failure

steps.label: Op log growth
steps.math: 2 M/s ÷ 4 = 0.5 M/s average × 86 400 s = 43.2 B ops/day × 100 B
steps.result: ≈ 4.3 TB/day of raw ops, ≈ 130 TB per 30 days

steps.label: Hottest single document
steps.math: 200 editors × 1 msg/s = 200 ops/s in; 200 × 199 ≈ 40 k deliveries/s out
steps.result: One owner process per doc is fine for ops. Fan-out is the hot path.

estimates.takeaway: Per-document load is tiny, even for a 200-person doc, so one owner process per document can order every op without locks. The scale problem is the number of documents and connections, solved by sharding docs across owners. The op log grows by terabytes per day, so we cannot keep every keystroke forever: snapshots plus a 30-day op tail, with older history compacted into revisions.

api.note: Initial load. Client starts at the returned rev. Served via CDN-cacheable snapshot plus a short tail from the op log.
Auth and permission check at connect. The gateway routes the socket to the doc's owner.

api.returns: ack { clientSeq, rev } | broadcast { rev, author, ops[] }
api.note: (clientId, clientSeq) makes resends idempotent after a reconnect. At most one unacked batch in flight per client.
Not persisted. Throttled to 5/s on the client, dropped first under load.
Restore is a new forward op that rewrites content, so collaborators stay in sync and nothing is erased.

entities.name: Op
entities.store: Wide-column store (Cassandra/Bigtable style), partition = docId, clustering = rev
entities.why: Append-only, read as a range 'ops for doc X after rev N'. Partition per doc keeps the range scan on one node.

entities.name: Snapshot
entities.store: Object storage, pointer in metadata DB
entities.why: Loading = newest snapshot + ops after its rev. Old snapshots double as browsable revisions.

entities.name: DocMeta
entities.why: Small, relational, transactional. Used on open and for permission checks.

entities.name: Presence
entities.store: In memory on the doc owner only
entities.why: Ephemeral. Losing it on failover costs one heartbeat of flicker, so it is never written to disk.

data.note: The op log is the source of truth; snapshots are a cache of 'ops 1..N applied'. The log is keyed by (docId, rev) with a uniqueness rule on rev, so two owners can never both write rev 5001 (a conditional insert acts as a fence). A snapshotter writes a new snapshot every 500 ops or 10 minutes of activity. Ops older than 30 days and older than the newest snapshot are compacted: we keep periodic snapshots as revisions and drop the keystroke-level ops between them.

hld.summary:
Clients keep a full local copy and apply their own edits immediately. They hold a WebSocket to a gateway, which looks up the document's owner in a routing table (consistent hashing over doc ids, plus a lease so only one owner is active). The owner keeps the document in memory, puts every incoming op in a single order, transforms it against anything the client had not seen, appends it to the op log, and only then acks the author and broadcasts to the other editors.

A snapshotter reads the log and writes compacted snapshots to object storage so documents open fast and owners can restart quickly. Presence travels through the same owner but is never stored. Everything that is not live editing (doc list, sharing, comments, history browsing) is plain REST against a metadata service.

diagram.title: Live editing path
diagram.src:
flowchart LR
  A[Editor A] --> GW[WebSocket gateways]
  B[Editor B] --> GW
  GW --> RT[Routing table with leases]
  GW --> OW[Doc owner, one per doc]
  OW --> LOG[(Op log)]
  OW --> GW
  LOG --> SN[Snapshotter]
  SN --> OBJ[(Snapshot store)]
  A --> API[Doc REST API]
  API --> META[(Doc metadata)]
  API --> OBJ
  API --> LOG

flows.title: Typing a character
steps: Editor applies the insert locally and adds it to its pending buffer.
Every 100 ms the client sends one batch tagged with baseRev (the last server rev it has seen) and clientSeq.
Owner transforms the batch against ops with rev greater than baseRev, assigns the next rev, and appends to the op log.
After the durable write, owner acks the author with the new rev and broadcasts the transformed op to other editors.
Other clients transform the incoming op against their own pending, unacked ops, then apply it.

flows.title: Opening a document
steps: Client calls GET /docs/{id}: permission check, then newest snapshot and the ops after it.
Client replays the tail locally to reach headRev.
Client opens the WebSocket with lastRev = headRev. The owner sends any ops that landed in between and the current presence list.

flows.title: Owner failover
steps: Owner process dies. Its lease expires after about 5 s.
Routing assigns the doc to a new owner, which loads the snapshot plus op tail from the log.
Clients reconnect with lastRev and resend unacked batches. clientSeq dedupe drops anything the old owner already wrote.

deepDives.title: OT vs CRDT, with a tiny example
deepDives.problem: Doc is abc. Alice inserts X at index 2 (abXc). At the same time Bob deletes index 0 (bc). If each side naively applies the other's op: Bob does insert(2, X) on bc and gets bcX. Alice does delete(0) on abXc and gets bXc. They have diverged. Positions are only meaningful relative to the state they were made against.

options.name: Operational Transformation (OT), server-ordered
options.how: Server picks one order. Each op is rewritten against concurrent ops that were ordered before it. Here Bob's delete is ordered first, so Alice's insert(2, X) becomes insert(1, X) because a character before position 2 vanished. Bob applies insert(1, X) to bc and gets bXc, same as Alice.
pros: Ops stay small (position + text), no per-character metadata
With a central server you only need transforms against one linear history, which is much easier to get right
Mature for rich text
cons: Correctness lives in the transform functions. Every new op type (tables, lists) needs transforms against every other type
Needs a server or a total order. Peer-to-peer OT is notoriously hard
Long offline sessions mean transforming thousands of ops at once

options.name: Sequence CRDT
options.how: Every character gets a unique id like (site, counter). An insert says 'put X after character id b1', not 'at index 2'. A delete marks a character id as a tombstone. Bob's delete of a1 and Alice's insert after b1 touch different ids, so they commute and any order gives bXc.
pros: Merge needs no server and no shared base, so long offline and peer-to-peer work
Works with end-to-end encryption because clients merge
Convergence is a property of the data type, easier to test
cons: Per-character ids and tombstones: memory and payload can be several times the text size without run-length compression
Interleaving anomalies when two people type at the same spot need extra rules
Garbage-collecting tombstones needs agreement that every replica has seen them

options.name: Locking sections (no merge)
options.how: A user takes a lock on a paragraph before editing it. Others see it as read-only.
pros: Trivial to build and reason about
cons: Not real co-editing: two people cannot fix typos in the same paragraph
Stale locks after crashes need timeouts

deepDives.choice: For this problem, with an always-available central service and offline windows of minutes to hours, I pick server-ordered OT: every op gets a dense rev from the doc owner, clients have at most one unacked batch, and the server transforms against one linear history. That keeps payloads and memory small and keeps history a simple numbered log. I would switch to a CRDT if the product requires end-to-end encryption, multi-day offline editing, or local-first sync between devices without our servers. A modern CRDT can still use the server as a relay and ordering point for history, so the rest of this design survives that change.

diagram.title: Server-ordered OT for the abc example
diagram.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant A as Alice
  participant S as Doc owner
  participant B as Bob
  Note over A,B: all at rev 7, doc is abc
  A->>A: apply insert 2 X, shows abXc
  B->>B: apply delete 0, shows bc
  B->>S: delete 0, baseRev 7
  A->>S: insert 2 X, baseRev 7
  S->>S: Bob arrived first, assign rev 8
  S-->>B: ack rev 8
  S-->>A: rev 8 delete 0
  A->>A: delete 0 is left of pending insert, apply it, shows bXc
  S->>S: transform Alice against rev 8, becomes insert 1 X, rev 9
  S-->>A: ack rev 9
  S-->>B: rev 9 insert 1 X
  B->>B: apply, shows bXc

deepDives.title: The server's role: one owner per document
deepDives.problem: OT needs a single order of ops per document. If two servers each accept edits for the same doc and assign revs, you get two histories that cannot be merged. We also need to survive the owner crashing without losing acked edits or forking history.

options.name: Single owner process per doc with a lease
options.how: Consistent hashing maps docId to an owner. A lease in a coordination store (etcd or ZooKeeper) confirms it. The owner holds the doc in memory, orders ops, writes to the log, broadcasts.
pros: Ordering is a single-threaded loop: no locks, no distributed consensus per keystroke
Transform and broadcast use in-memory state, so latency stays low
cons: Hot docs cannot be split
Failover takes a lease timeout (a few seconds) of editing pause
Needs fencing so a paused old owner cannot write after losing the lease

options.name: Stateless servers, compare-and-set on the log
options.how: Any server can handle an op. It reads ops since baseRev from the DB, transforms, and does a conditional insert at rev N+1. On conflict it retries.
pros: No routing or leases
Any server failure is invisible
cons: Every keystroke reads from the DB
A doc with 50 active editors thrashes on retries
Broadcast needs a separate pub/sub per doc anyway

options.name: Pure relay, clients merge (CRDT style)
options.how: Server only relays and stores ops. Clients merge everything.
pros: Server is simple and scales horizontally
cons: Only works with a CRDT
Server cannot validate or reject malformed ops without understanding them

deepDives.choice: Single owner per doc with a lease. The numbers say even the worst doc does about 200 ops/s, so one thread per doc is plenty and the hard part is spreading 1.5 M open docs across, say, 200 owner processes (≈ 7.5 k docs each). Fencing: the op log insert is conditional on rev not existing, and each owner stamps its lease epoch, so a zombie owner's write fails. I would revisit only if single docs grew to thousands of simultaneous editors; then I'd split the document into independently ordered sections.

deepDives.title: Cursors and presence
deepDives.problem: Cursor positions are indexes, so they go stale the moment someone else types above them. Presence is also chatty: 2 M sessions moving cursors would double message volume. And it must not slow down real edits.

options.name: Through the doc owner, tagged with a rev
options.how: Client sends { rev, anchor, head }. Owner and receivers transform the cursor through ops between that rev and their current rev, just like an insert at that point.
pros: Cursors land in the right spot even mid-burst
Same connection, no extra system
cons: Presence traffic shares the owner's loop with ops
Must be throttled and dropped under load

options.name: Separate pub/sub channel (Redis per doc)
options.how: Gateways publish cursor updates to a channel per doc. Receivers place cursors using their local text.
pros: Isolates presence load from editing
Owner failure does not affect presence
cons: Cursor and op ordering can disagree, so cursors jump
One more system on the hot path

deepDives.choice: Route presence through the owner but treat it as lowest priority: client throttles to 5 updates/s and only sends on change; owner coalesces per user (keeps only the latest) and drops presence before ever delaying ops. Cursors are anchored to a rev and transformed like zero-width inserts. Presence expires after 30 s without a heartbeat and is never persisted. If presence ever dominated owner CPU (huge view-only audiences), I would move viewers' presence to a separate sampled channel and show '120 viewers' instead of 120 cursors.

deepDives.title: Snapshots plus an op log, and version history
deepDives.problem: Replaying a document from its first keystroke is too slow for a two-year-old doc with millions of ops. Storing a full copy per change wastes storage. History must still let users jump to 'yesterday at 3 pm'.

options.name: Op log only
options.how: Rebuild any state by replaying ops from rev 0.
pros: Perfect history, simplest writes
cons: Open time grows forever
4.3 TB/day kept forever

options.name: Snapshot only, on every save
options.how: Overwrite the full document on each change.
pros: Fast open
cons: No op-level sync for live editing
Write amplification: 50 KB per keystroke

options.name: Periodic snapshots plus a bounded op log
options.how: Snapshot every 500 ops or 10 minutes. Open = latest snapshot + tail. Keep keystroke ops for 30 days; beyond that keep hourly or daily snapshots as revisions.
pros: Open cost bounded by about 500 ops
Fine-grained recent history, coarse old history
Owner restart is fast
cons: Snapshotter is another moving part
Old history loses per-keystroke authorship detail

deepDives.choice: Periodic snapshots plus a bounded op log. Snapshot writes are cheap: 500 ops per snapshot means snapshot traffic is 1/500 of op traffic. The snapshotter is a separate consumer so it never slows the owner. Restore is a forward op, not a rewind, so live collaborators stay consistent. If legal hold or audit requires every keystroke, we would tier old ops to cold object storage instead of dropping them; that is a cost decision, not a design change.

deepDives.title: Offline edits
deepDives.problem: A user edits on a plane for two hours while colleagues keep editing online. On reconnect, hundreds of local ops based on rev 4 000 must merge with thousands of server ops up to rev 9 000, without losing either side's work.

options.name: Queue and rebase on reconnect (OT)
options.how: Client persists pending ops in IndexedDB with baseRev. On reconnect it fetches ops since baseRev, transforms its pending ops against them locally, and sends the rebased batch.
pros: Reuses the normal OT path
Server work is bounded: client does the transforming
cons: Cost grows with both sides' op counts
Large structural edits can merge in surprising ways (text into a deleted section)

options.name: CRDT state sync
options.how: Client and server exchange version vectors and send only missing ops. Merge is automatic.
pros: Any offline duration works
No rebase step
cons: Requires CRDT everywhere
Tombstones from long offline periods are hard to garbage-collect

options.name: Fork and ask the user
options.how: If offline work exceeds a threshold, save it as a branch and show a compare view.
pros: No silent surprises for large conflicts
cons: Worse experience, manual work

deepDives.choice: Use queue and rebase as the default: pending ops survive tab closes in IndexedDB, and the client rebases against the server's ops since its baseRev before sending. Add a safety valve: if the gap is larger than about 5 000 ops or the client was offline more than 7 days, save the offline work as a named revision and merge, so the user can always recover their version. If offline-for-days became a core use case, this is the trigger to move to a CRDT.

failures: Lease expires in about 5 s, new owner loads snapshot plus op tail. Clients resend unacked batches. (clientId, clientSeq) dedupe prevents double inserts.
Old owner is paused by GC, loses its lease, then wakes and writes
Log insert is conditional on the rev slot being empty and stamped with lease epoch. The zombie's write fails and it drops its sessions.
Op log store slow or unavailable
Owner stops acking, so clients keep ops pending locally and show 'saving…'. No ack is ever sent before a durable write.
A client sends a malformed or malicious op
Owner validates op ranges against current length and permissions before applying. Reject and force that client to reload from snapshot.
Opens get slower because the op tail is longer, but nothing is lost. Alert on tail length per doc above 2 000 ops.
Gateway zone outage drops 30% of connections at once
Clients reconnect with jittered backoff. Owners stay up, so reconnect is a cheap 'ops since lastRev' replay.
scale: 10× users: more owners and gateways. Routing is consistent hashing, so add nodes and move a fraction of docs. Op log is partitioned by docId and scales out linearly.
Giant docs (1 000+ editors): split the doc into sections each with its own ordering, and send view-only users a throttled stream of snapshots instead of every op.
Global teams: place each doc's owner in the region of most of its editors and move it when that changes. Cross-region editors pay one extra round trip (≈ 150 ms) but still see local typing instantly.
Storage: tier op logs older than a week to cheaper storage and compact aggressively. Snapshots dedupe well because most docs are small and change slowly.

followups.q: How do you guarantee two clients end up identical?
answer: The server's rev order is the single truth. Every client applies the same ops in rev order, after transforming its own pending ops.
Transforms must satisfy the property that applying A then transformed B equals applying B then transformed A. Property-based tests with random concurrent ops check it.
Clients periodically send a hash of their content at a rev. A mismatch triggers a reload and an alert.

followups.q: How does undo work when other people are editing?
answer: Undo is local: it undoes my last op, not the document's last op.
Build the inverse of my op and transform it through everything that happened since, then send it as a new forward op.
If my text was already deleted by someone else, the inverse becomes a no-op.

followups.q: How would you add suggestions (track changes)?
answer: Model a suggestion as a formatting attribute on ranges (suggested-insert, suggested-delete) with an author.
Accept or reject is just another op that removes the attribute or the text.
Transforms already handle attributes, so no new ordering machinery.

followups.q: What if the network reorders or duplicates messages?
answer: WebSocket over TCP keeps order per connection. Across reconnects, the rev and clientSeq numbers repair it.
Client drops any broadcast with rev not equal to its current rev + 1 and asks for the gap.
Duplicates are dropped by (clientId, clientSeq) on the server and by rev on clients.

followups.q: How do you handle permissions changing mid-session?
answer: Permission check on connect, plus the owner subscribes to ACL changes for its docs.
On revoke, owner closes that user's socket and rejects further ops.
Ops already acked stay. Revocation is not retroactive.

mistakes: Saying 'last write wins' for text. It throws away one person's typing.
Waiting for the server before showing a local keystroke. Typing must be optimistic.
Letting any server accept ops for any doc, which forks history.
Persisting every cursor movement, or sending cursors as bare indexes without a rev.
Naming CRDTs without saying their cost (metadata and tombstones) or why you would or would not need them here.

mid: Asked about rich text, max editors per doc, and offline duration before designing
Applied local edits optimistically and used WebSockets for live updates
Stored documents as snapshots plus a log of changes
Showed the abc example (or similar) where naive positions diverge
senior: Explained one OT transform or CRDT merge concretely, with positions
Gave each doc a single ordering point and explained routing to it
Acked ops only after a durable write and deduped resends with a client sequence number
Anchored cursors to a rev and throttled presence, without persisting it
Sized the op log (TB/day) and chose snapshot cadence from it
staff: Chose OT or CRDT from requirements (E2E encryption, offline length) and named the trigger to switch
Handled owner failover with leases and fencing so a zombie owner cannot fork history
Planned history compaction and retention with a concrete storage number
Covered offline rebase cost and a safety valve for huge divergence
